name: The Unmaking Hour

detectability.signature: Paradoxical tachyon backwash — sensor returns arrive before the query is sent, and threat indicators trigger for impacts that have not yet occurred

proximity: Onboard clocks desynchronize by seconds per minute
Crew report déjà vu and phantom radio chatter from voices they have not yet heard
contact: Vessels flicker between two timelines, hulls aging decades in moments
Cause and effect invert — damage appears on the hull before the impact that causes it
prolonged_exposure: Causality collapse: crew members cease to have ever existed, erased from records and memory alike
The local timeline unravels into recursive self-destruction loops with no stable exit

phenomena: Radio signals arriving before being sent
Visible echoes of past events replaying in open space
Objects existing in multiple timeframes simultaneously
opportunities: Communication with other times and possibly other realities
Unique research opportunity for temporal physicists
known_incidents: The colony ship Meridian Dawn transmitted a detailed distress call eleven years before it ever launched
Survey team Kestrel returned from a four-hour sortie having aged ninety years, minus two members who appear in no crew manifest
description: There is nothing to see at the Unmaking Hour — no glow, no distortion, no shadow — which is precisely what makes it lethal. Instruments scream instead: sensor returns arriving before their queries, collision alarms sounding for debris strikes that happen minutes later. The zone spans nearly two astronomical units of space where cause and effect have quietly stopped agreeing on the order of things.

The fracture pulses on a rough nineteen-minute cycle, though the pulse arrives early, late, or twice depending on which observer you ask. Vessels crossing the boundary begin to flicker between states — new paint peeling to rust and back, crews glimpsing their own funerals. Prolonged presence does not merely kill; it edits, removing people and ships from history until even their loved ones cannot say what was lost.

No one knows what broke here. The leading theory holds that some pre-cursor civilization's experiment fractured local causality beyond repair, but the zone predates every artifact in the region. The Meridian Dawn incident made the fracture infamous: a colony ship answering its own future distress call, flying into the very disaster it would someday suffer.

The fracture remains unquarantined because it cannot be reliably mapped — its boundaries shift with each pulse, and exclusion buoys have been found inside themselves. Temporal physicists pay fortunes for edge telemetry, and at least three research vessels are listed as overdue. Pilots crossing the sector watch their clocks, and pray the second hand keeps moving forward.
